doc.title: Young Snooky — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Ellington trumpeters Cootie Williams, Ray Nance and Bubber Miley
summary: Young describes Cootie Williams' side-of-the-mouth playing, Ray Nance's dancing and violin, and Bubber Miley's plunger work.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: I said, we‘re going to get him. But ok, what about Cootie, what about Cootie Williams?

Cootie Williams, he was a very strong trumpet player and he played way over here on the side of his mouth. Cootie Williams, well, he was something else and Duke Ellington‘s band, man, Cootie was, man. He was, Cootie and that other little old trumpet player in Duke‘s band. Used to dance and get up and…
Oh, are you talking about Ray Nance?

And he played violin. Ray Nance, man. He was a nice cat, man, but he fooled around with some wrong stuff and took him away from here too. Ray Nance, Ray Nance and there was another trumpet player in Duke‘s band… Cootie Williams, Ray Nance…
Bubber Miley, but that‘s way back.

Bubber Miley, I don‘t know too much about Bubber, Bubber was something else. I wish I could tell you something about Bubber Miley, but I can‘t, all I can tell you is I remember that name, Bubber Miley. He must have been a good…

Plunger man. And then Cootie came in and took that away from him, because Cootie come in and play that plunger thing, man, he was something else. Cootie played way over on the side of his mouth when he played, but he could play, man.
